Consider carefully: If you only want to develop or tune a single system, are unwilling to maintain data models and standards, struggle with major changes to plans following security or compliance feedback, or are unwilling to invest time in architecture documents, tradeoff rationales and review records, actual work will differ from your expectations.

The core output is data architecture that can evolve over the long term: data models and logical/physical database descriptions, data classification and access-boundary explanations, storage and integration plans, backup and recovery targets, performance and capacity planning, and change and review records—not merely a database that is built and runs.

Low-risk check: Use a public or fictional scenario to draw a one-page data architecture for a fictional subscription product, list entities and data classifications, two storage options and access boundaries, and specify recovery targets, one failure condition and assumptions awaiting validation. Assess work preferences only. The exercise involves no real personal or production data and does not establish successful job training, data authorization or a hiring commitment.

The central question: Can you turn data models, storage and integration plans, access and recovery controls, and change standards into architecture that can be reviewed, validated and handed over while business needs, data classification and compliance constraints, performance and cost budgets, and long-term evolution requirements all apply?

Work is mainly office-based or remote, with long periods using modeling tools, documents and review meetings, and concentrated time pressure during migrations, deployments and incidents. Where are the boundaries between database architects and adjacent warehousing, operations and analysis roles?

This table compares database architects with adjacent data warehousing specialists, database administrators, data scientists, computer systems analysts, computer network architects, and computer systems engineers/architects across seven dimensions: core purpose, main objects and basis, core process, main outputs, responsible parties, collaboration and supervision, and limits of conclusions. All work with data and systems, but objects differ: cross-system data models and standards, warehouse modeling and loading, existing database operations and changes, analysis and modeling, business processes and systems requirements, or network and systems architecture. Adjacency does not transfer whether the role centers on enterprise data architecture design, standards and long-term evolution. Compare actual outputs and business process stages item by item.
Core purpose
Design architecture strategies and standards for enterprise databases, data warehouses and multidimensional networks so new systems can integrate into scalable, reliable data infrastructure.

Core purposes of adjacent roles: Data warehousing specialists design and implement warehousing and loading; database administrators ensure existing database availability and access control; data scientists build and validate analytical models from data; computer systems analysts analyze business needs and design systems; computer network architects design network architecture and connectivity; computer systems engineers/architects design and integrate systems and architectures.
Main objects and basis

Enterprise databases and warehouses, multidimensional networks, data models and classifications, operating and security standards, storage and integration plans. The basis is business and compliance needs, architecture standards and change approval procedures, and organizational information management rules.

Objects and basis of adjacent roles: Dimension and fact tables and loading workflows (data warehousing specialists); database structures and operating parameters (database administrators); datasets and evaluation metrics (data scientists); business processes and systems requirements (computer systems analysts); network topologies, bandwidth and security domains (computer network architects); system components and integration interfaces (computer systems engineers/architects).
Core process

Clarify business and compliance needs → Inventory data and dependencies → Build logical and physical models → Select storage and integration options → Define access, backup and recovery controls → Test and improve continuously.

Processes of adjacent roles: Model and build loading and quality workflows (data warehousing specialists); execute changes and maintain operations (database administrators); clean data, model and validate (data scientists); organize requirements and design systems (computer systems analysts); plan and implement networks and security domains (computer network architects); design and integrate systems and interfaces (computer systems engineers/architects).
Main outputs

Architecture documents and data models, storage and integration plans, data classifications and access boundaries, backup and recovery targets, performance and capacity planning, and change and review records.

Outputs of adjacent roles: Warehouse models and loading workflows (data warehousing specialists); change and operating records (database administrators); reproducible analyses and models (data scientists); requirements and systems design documents (computer systems analysts); network architecture and implementation records (computer network architects); systems architecture and integration plans (computer systems engineers/architects).
Responsible parties

People in this occupation are responsible for architectural soundness, standards consistency and long-term evolvability. Corresponding authorized personnel decide data-use authorization, production change approval and security exceptions. High-impact changes and cross-domain migrations require approval and reporting under procedures, not unilateral decisions by database architects.

Responsible parties in adjacent roles: Data warehousing specialists are responsible for warehouse models and loading quality; database administrators for database availability and access control; data scientists for method and validation reliability; computer systems analysts for requirements and systems design; computer network architects for network architecture and connectivity; computer systems engineers/architects for systems architecture and integration.
Collaboration and supervision

Core tasks include collaboration across architecture and project teams. Check actual reporting relationships, change permissions and escalation procedures for the job. No nationally uniform architecture-committee reporting relationship has been verified.

Collaboration in adjacent roles: Data warehousing specialists work with business and data governance teams; database administrators with application and operations teams; data scientists with business and engineering teams; computer systems analysts with business and development teams; computer network architects with operations and security teams; computer systems engineers/architects with engineering and integration teams.
Limits of conclusions

Editorial comparison of main objects in databases/warehousing, analysis, systems, networks and engineering. Responsibilities may overlap; DBAs also model and set standards. Occupational titles cannot establish absolute mutual exclusion or uniform assessment criteria.
Preparation levels and practice requirements for adjacent roles do not apply to this occupation. Check each against official occupational information and the actual job's requirements.
Key professional judgments

Six recurring professional judgments: Have data semantics and dependencies been clarified? Have data classification, purposes and access boundaries been checked? Do models and storage plans explain tradeoffs among consistency, performance and costs? Have changes and migrations been reviewed, made reversible and independently validated? Have backup and recovery targets been validated through drills? Are semantic errors, overly broad permissions or unclear impacts met with a pause, recheck and escalation?

Editorial check suggestion: Clarify business meanings, field semantics, upstream/downstream dependencies and lifecycles before design. Semantic misunderstandings entering models, interfaces or reports may cause rework. Actual frequency and long-term costs have not been verified.

Determine access boundaries, retention requirements and migration scope by data classification and purposes. Mixing restricted data into broadly accessible areas creates both compliance and security risks.

Editorial check suggestion: Record tradeoffs among consistency, latency, scalability, costs and operational complexity, and their basis. Missing records may hinder reviews after requirements change, not make reviews entirely impossible.

Editorial check suggestion: For structure changes and cross-environment migration, check review, rollback and result-validation arrangements. Review personnel and division of work follow actual rules and authorization. Self-testing may miss biases, but is not incapable of finding systemic problems.
Judgment four: Have changes been reviewed and independently validated?

CISA recommends regular disaster-recovery tests of backup availability and integrity. Editors also suggest checking recovery times and targets. With successful backup-job records alone and no recovery validation, recovery capability is unproven, not necessarily impossible.
Judgment five: Have recovery targets been tested in drills?

When semantic errors, overly broad permissions, migration losses, performance bottlenecks, unverifiable backups or unclear data classifications/compliance boundaries arise, pause high-risk actions, recheck facts, preserve records and report under organizational rules.

Architecture strategy and requirements | Clarify requirements and develop strategies | Collaborate with systems architects, software architects and design analysts to understand business or industry needs, develop database architecture strategies during modeling, design and implementation, and write and archive database architecture.

Modeling and design | Design database structures and data models | Design databases supporting business applications to ensure scalability, security, performance and reliability, develop data models for applications, metadata tables, views or related structures, and document and communicate database schemas using accepted notation.

Storage and integration | Select options and integrate systems | Design interfaces, data transfer mechanisms, global temporary tables, data partitions and function-based indexes, develop integration methods across products, integrate new systems into existing warehouse structures, and improve performance and functionality.

Standards and governance | Set and enforce development standards | Create and enforce database development standards, identify and correct deviations, review project requests to estimate time and costs, and identify and assess database industry trends to advise senior management.

Reliability and performance | Set up backup/recovery and optimize | Set up database clusters, backup or recovery procedures, demonstrate technical database functions such as performance, security and reliability, develop load-balancing procedures to eliminate backup-related downtime, plan and install database management system upgrades, and identify, assess and recommend hardware/software achieving required performance.

Testing and support | Testing and error correction, application procedural code/query maintenance, and support for junior staff or clients are core. Training users and answering questions are supplemental, not duties everyone must perform.

values: Fictional architecture scenario materials (practice inputs)

Fictional scenario: a database architect encounters four problems within the same project cycle. First, the business team asks for customer data from three systems to be integrated into a unified model, but field meanings differ across systems. Second, to facilitate analysis, the team wants to copy production data containing personal information directly into the development environment. Third, a migration window has been scheduled, but the validation and rollback plans have not been verified. Fourth, key queries become noticeably slower after deployment, and the business team demands immediate indexing and capacity expansion.
Materials provided: business requirements and a data dictionary; data classification and access management rules; change and migration approval processes; capacity and performance targets.

Materials not provided: whose definition should prevail in a field semantics conflict, a compliant path for using restricted data in the development environment, whether migration may proceed in the original window when validation and rollback have not been verified, and the approval and validation requirements for adding indexes and expanding capacity. If you need these conditions for the exercise, explicitly state your assumptions and whom you need to confirm them with.
Task requirements

Write a one-page response and reporting plan covering checks and modeling responses for field semantics conflicts, a compliant path for restricted data to enter the development environment, prerequisites and validation requirements for executing the migration window, and the investigation sequence and approval boundaries for performance problems.

The plan must state which information comes from the scenario materials and which remains an assumption, and explain whether its basis is the data dictionary and modeling standards, data classification and access management rules, change and migration approval processes, or capacity and performance targets.
Reference deliverable (derivable from the scenario)

The plan should include: semantic conflicts (first confirm definitions field by field with business and system owners, retain source identifiers and mapping rules where necessary, and explicitly record disagreements in the model before proceeding, without overriding them with one side's definition); restricted data (do not directly copy production data; request masking or use fictional data under data classification and access management rules, and retain access records within the authorized scope); migration (do not execute in the original window before the validation and rollback plans have been verified; first complete drills and comparison rules, adjusting the window and reporting risks where necessary); performance (first locate bottlenecks and assess the affected scope, then evaluate the trade-offs and costs of indexes and capacity expansion, request approval through the change approval process, and implement after validation); handover (clearly document the status of all four matters, actions taken and items awaiting confirmation).
The reference deliverable lists only the elements to include; your wording need not match the example, as long as you can explain the basis for your judgments.
Boundaries and conclusions that cannot be inferred

This exercise only tests awareness of semantic conflict handling, data classification, migration safety and rollback, and change approval. It does not assess whether responses in real projects are compliant, and does not constitute compliance, security or legal advice.

Do not use real organizational data or nonpublic business materials. Actual processing of restricted data and personal information, production structure changes and migration across environments must follow organizational information management policies, data security and personal information protection regulations, and industry compliance requirements, with appropriate authorization obtained under current regulations where necessary.

entries.answer: Design strategies for enterprise databases, data warehouse systems and multidimensional networks: write and document database architecture; collaborate with system architects, software architects and design analysts to understand business or industry requirements; develop database architecture strategies during modeling, design and implementation; design databases supporting business applications to ensure scalability, security, performance and reliability; develop data models for applications, metadata tables, views or related structures; design interfaces, data transfer mechanisms, global temporary tables, data partitions and function-based indexes; develop integration methods between different products; create and enforce database development standards; document and communicate database schemas; coordinate database development and determine scope and limitations; identify and assess industry trends in database systems; set up database clusters, backup or recovery processes; demonstrate database technical functions; develop load-balancing processes to eliminate backup downtime; plan and install database management system software upgrades; evaluate and recommend software and hardware technologies; test and debug; identify and correct deviations from standards; review project requests to estimate time and cost; write logical and physical database descriptions; develop or maintain archiving processes, procedural code or queries for applications; provide technical support to junior staff or clients; determine optimal values for database parameters; and train users.
entries.question: What specifically do database architects do each day?

entries.answer: This occupation centers on designing architecture strategies and standards for enterprise databases, data warehouses and multidimensional networks, allowing new systems to integrate into scalable, reliable data infrastructure. Data warehousing specialists focus on warehouse modeling and loading; database administrators on operating, changing and controlling access to existing databases; data scientists on analytical and predictive modeling; computer systems analysts on business requirements analysis and system design; computer network architects on network architecture and connectivity solutions; and computer systems engineers and architects on system-level architecture and integration. entries.answer: Generative assistants can help draft schemas, explain SQL, map metadata, screen anomalies and check documentation. Automation and cloud platforms also perform some cluster deployment, parameter tuning, monitoring and alerting. However, generated drafts do not establish sound architecture, usable data or safe changes. People still need to take responsibility for data classification and purpose confirmation, permission and migration reviews, independent performance and recovery validation, records of models and human modifications, and production change approval. Technical capability does not equal organizational adoption, production authorization or occupational replacement. O*NET shows that 48% in this occupation consider accuracy and precision 'extremely important', 43% consider the consequences of errors 'serious', and 52% face time pressure once a week or more. Technical exposure does not equal organizational adoption or job disappearance, and cannot be interpreted as the probability of job loss.

description.text: Database architects (O*NET-SOC 15-1243.00, Bright Outlook) design strategies for enterprise databases, data warehouse systems and multidimensional networks. Tasks include developing standards for database operations, programming, queries and security; modeling and building large relational databases or data warehouses; creating and optimizing data models for warehouse infrastructure and workflows; writing and documenting database architecture; collaborating with system and software architects to understand requirements; designing databases supporting business applications to ensure scalability, security and reliability; developing data models and database applications (interfaces, data transfer, partitions and function-based indexes); creating and enforcing database development standards; setting up clusters and backup/recovery processes; developing load balancing to eliminate backup downtime; planning and installing database management system upgrades; evaluating and recommending software and hardware technologies; testing and debugging; reviewing project requests to estimate time and cost; determining optimal database parameter values; and training users. Its U.S. employment and wage scope must be explained: this occupation is O*NET-SOC 15-1243.00 itself, with approximately 66,900 employed in 2024, projected growth of 9% during 2024–2034 (labeled 'Much faster than average', Bright Outlook), approximately 72,700 people projected in 2034, and approximately 4,000 average annual openings including growth and replacement over the projection period. In 2025 wage data, median annual pay is 139,500 dollars (median hourly pay 67.07 dollars), with annual wage percentiles 86,240/109,370/139,500/169,290/204,000 dollars. Industries are professional, scientific and technical services 36%/finance and insurance 16%/information 13%/other industries (including enterprise management and administrative support services) 35%. Interest code CI, preparation level Job Zone Four. Also address the occupational wage gap for such mainland China roles, labeling of the information transmission, software and information technology services industry-average proxy, and control points for data classification, minimum permissions, change review, independent validation, offline encrypted backups and recovery drills.

subject.name: Database architect
subject.summary: In the United States, database architects correspond to O*NET-SOC 15-1243.00 (Database Architects), designing strategies for enterprise databases, data warehouse systems and multidimensional networks: develop standards for database operations, programming, query processes and security; model, design and build large relational databases or data warehouses; create and optimize data models for warehouse infrastructure and workflows; integrate new systems with existing warehouse structures; and improve system performance and functionality. Work includes writing and documenting database architecture; collaborating with system architects, software architects, design analysts and others to understand business or industry requirements; developing database architecture strategies during modeling, design and implementation; designing databases supporting business applications to ensure scalability, security, performance and reliability; developing data models for applications, metadata tables, views or related structures; designing database applications (such as interfaces, data transfer mechanisms, global temporary tables, data partitions and function-based indexes) to support efficient access to general database structures; developing integration methods between products; creating and enforcing database development standards; documenting and communicating database schemas using accepted notation; developing data models describing data elements and their uses according to processes; coordinating database development as a project team member and determining project scope and limitations; identifying and assessing database system industry trends and providing information and recommendations to senior management; setting up database clusters, backup or recovery processes; demonstrating database technical functions (such as performance, security and reliability); developing load-balancing processes to eliminate downtime caused by backups; planning and installing database management system software upgrades to improve performance; identifying, evaluating and recommending hardware or software technologies that meet required performance; testing programs or databases, correcting errors and making necessary modifications; identifying and correcting deviations from database development standards; reviewing project requests describing database user needs to estimate required time and cost; writing logical and physical database descriptions and specifying identifiers, or directing others to do so; developing or maintaining archiving processes, procedural code or queries for applications; providing technical support to junior staff or clients; using manuals and computational tools to determine and calculate optimal database parameter values; and training users and answering questions. The preparation level is Job Zone Four (considerable preparation needed, SVP 7.0 to below 8.0). The official education survey shows that among new entrants, 76% require a bachelor's degree, 14% a master's degree and 5% a postsecondary certificate. On O*NET, this detailed occupation's tasks, work contexts, preparation level and wages concern the occupation itself: its 2025 national wages page publishes both annual and hourly percentiles, without labeling a parent occupation or opaque proxy, and it is not the related data warehousing specialist or database administrator occupation. O*NET labels this occupation Bright Outlook (2024–2034 growth 9%, much faster than average). Similar roles in China are commonly database architecture, data platform or data architecture positions; their duties, employment and pay definitions do not correspond one-to-one to this detailed U.S. occupation and are not interchangeable.
